newsitem.title: USA: Dow rallies after Friday's big decline.
newsitem.headline: Dow rallies after Friday's big decline.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks rebounded strongly on Monday as bargain hunters surfaced after the Dow Jones industrial average fell to its second-biggest point loss ever Friday.

The world's most widely watched stock index rose 108.70 points, or 1.4 percent, to 7,803.36, regaining almost half of Friday's 247-point decline, which was the biggest percentage drop in nearly six years.

Despite the recovery in the 30-share Dow, many investors remained unsure of the market's short-term direction. In broader trading, declining issues led advances by a narrow margin, 1,461 to 1,393, on active volume of 514 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Analysts said blue-chip issues raced higher as investors sought bargains in well-known corporate names after Friday's sell-off. Wall Street was also bracing for Tuesday's Federal Reserve policy-makers' meeting on interest rates, though the betting was the central bank would hold rates steady.
"This was a very good first step" after Friday's losses, said Brad Weekes, managing director of equity trading at Donaldson, Lufkin Jenrette & Co.
Despite Friday's drop, money managers saw little sign that assets were being reallocated in investment portfolios.

"We have not seen any and we don't intend to make any," said James Walline, vice president, equities and mutual funds at Lutheran Brotherhood. "The market has stabilized this morning and frankly we don't see any reason to reallocate."
A strong bond market, a stable dollar and the underlying belief that the economy was still in good shape helped fuel Monday's rebound, Weekes said.
The market was also relieved that it did not have to battle the expiration of futures and options, which added to Friday's rout.
The Dow started the day with a gain of 30 points before lurching 76 points lower as investors switched into the less-volatile bond market.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury rose 11/32, or $3.44 on a $1,000 bond, lowering its yield to 6.52 percent from 6.55 percent Friday. Prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Blue-chips stocks fared better in the recovery than their smaller counterparts.
"We still have fears of slower corporate growth, but a lot of those big-name blue-chip stocks have fallen a good deal," said Scott Bleier, chief market strategist for Prime Charter Limited.
Wall Street has begun to worry about whether one of the engines driving the bull market -- strong corporate earnings -- has begun to sputter after several profit warnings from high-profile companies.
On Monday, the earnings punch came from Hewlett-Packard Co., which reported disappointing quarterly results due to slow sales of medical equipment and higher costs. Its stock fell 2-3/4 to 63-5/16.

Consumer products giant Gillette Co. and its rival Procter & Gamble Co. fell after Friday's news that Gillette expected slower profit growth. Gillette fell 2-7/8 to 83 and Procter & Gamble lost 1-9/16 to 135.

Multinationals and drug stocks rose as bargain hunters stepped in to buy the stocks at lower levels. General Electric surged 3-1/8 to 65-7/8, Merck & Co. rose 2-5/16 to 93-1/8, and Johnson & Johnson added 2-1/8 to 58-1/16.
The Nasdaq composite index rose 7.49 points to 1,569.52.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 11.68 to 912.49. The American Stock Exchange index slipped 0.92 to 634.59.
The NYSE composite index of all listed common stocks rose 4.45 to 473.55. The average share was up 42 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 8,708.576 up 77.213 or 0.89 percent.
